passage.title: Modern Britain: A Diverse Nation
paras: Britain has welcomed newcomers for two thousand years. Romans, Saxons, Vikings and Normans all crossed the sea and settled here. From 1685 onwards, thousands of Huguenot refugees fled France and made new lives in London, many as weavers and silversmiths.

In 1948, HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury, bringing people from the Caribbean who had been invited to help rebuild the country after the Second World War. In the 1950s and 1960s, families arrived from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and in 1972 Asians expelled from Uganda resettled in Britain. Each group brought skills, food, faith and stories that are now part of everyday British life.

Every ten years, the census counts everyone in the country. The 2021 Census counted everyone in England and Wales on one day in March. It showed a nation of many faiths: about 3.9 million people (6.5%) described themselves as Muslim, and millions more as Christian, Hindu, Sikh, Jewish or of no religion.

Many languages are spoken in homes. After English, the most common main languages were Polish (1.1% of people), Romanian (0.8%), Panjabi (0.5%) and Urdu (0.5%). Yet most people say English is their main language: about nine in ten.
Numbers cannot tell us everything. A census records who lives here, but not whether people feel they belong. That story is told by the people themselves.

questions.q: Summarise the article in one sentence of no more than 20 words
questions.a: For example: Britain has always welcomed newcomers, and today its people speak many languages and follow many faiths.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a PEEDL paragraph: 'Compare how the poem and the article present Britain as a diverse society.' Starter: 'Both texts present Britain as..., but...'
questions.a: A PEEDL paragraph: both show a mixed nation; the article uses dates and data, the poem a recipe metaphor and a call for justice.

questions.q: Extend: complete the comparison grid with three similarities or differences
questions.a: For example: purpose (inform / persuade); method (data / metaphor); tone (neutral / warm and humorous).

questions.q: Stretch: what can a census not tell us about belonging?
questions.a: It counts people but cannot show whether they feel welcome; that needs voices like Zephaniah's.

questions.q: What is the main difference in purpose between the article and the poem?
options: the article informs with facts; the poem persuades through a metaphor
questions.a: C) the article informs with facts; the poem persuades through a metaphor. The article uses data to inform; the poem uses a recipe to make readers value fairness.

questions.q: Answer the ponder: can numbers tell us what belonging feels like?
questions.a: For example: no; they show who is here, but feelings need personal voices.
